scenario: A team lead wrote the team's lint and naming conventions in their own ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md. Claude Code follows them in the lead's sessions, but a new developer who cloned the repository last week finds that Claude ignores them entirely.
question: What should the team change?

options.text: Ask the new developer to copy the lead's ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md onto their own machine.
Move the conventions into the project's CLAUDE.md and commit it to the repository.
Put the conventions in a CLAUDE.local.md file at the root of the repository.
Tell Claude to remember the conventions, so they are saved in auto memory.

explanation.correct: User-level instructions in ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md apply only to that user. Team conventions belong in the project CLAUDE.md (./CLAUDE.md or ./.claude/CLAUDE.md), which is shared with everyone through version control.

distractors.A: Copying works for one person but drifts as soon as the lead edits their file, and it repeats for every new hire.
distractors.C: CLAUDE.local.md is for personal, project-specific notes and is meant to be gitignored, so teammates never get it.
distractors.D: Auto memory is notes Claude keeps for one user. It is not shared with teammates.

scenario: A developer wants Claude Code to know their personal sandbox URL and test account for one project. These details apply only to them and only to this repository, and they must never be committed.
question: Where should the developer put them?

options.text: In the project's CLAUDE.md, under a heading marked as personal notes.
In ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, so they are kept outside the repository.
In a rule file at .claude/rules/sandbox.md inside the project.
In CLAUDE.local.md at the project root, listed in .gitignore.

explanation.correct: CLAUDE.local.md holds personal, project-specific instructions. It loads alongside the project CLAUDE.md, and once it is in .gitignore it never reaches the repository.

distractors.A: The project CLAUDE.md is committed and shared, so every teammate would get the private details.
distractors.B: User-level instructions load in every project, not just this one.
distractors.C: .claude/rules/ is part of the project configuration and is normally committed, so it would be shared too.

scenario: In a monorepo, shared standards live in docs/standards/: api.md, testing.md, and frontend.md. The payments package needs only api.md and testing.md, and its maintainers want its CLAUDE.md to include exactly those, staying in sync as the standards change.
question: What is the best way to do this?

options.text: Import the two files with @ paths, relative to the package's CLAUDE.md.
Paste every standards file into the root CLAUDE.md so all packages see them all.
Copy api.md and testing.md into the payments package and edit the copies there.
Move all three standards files into one skill that each package can invoke.

explanation.correct: CLAUDE.md can import files with @path/to/file. Relative paths resolve from the file that contains the import, imports can nest up to four levels, and the imported content stays in sync with its source.

distractors.B: Loading every standard into every package wastes context and gives payments the frontend rules it does not need.
distractors.C: Copies drift from the shared standards as soon as either one changes.
distractors.D: Standards that should always apply belong in always-loaded instructions. A skill loads only when it is invoked or judged relevant.

scenario: The root CLAUDE.md says "Indent with 2 spaces." The legacy services/payments/CLAUDE.md says "Indent with 4 spaces." A developer starts Claude Code at the repository root and asks it to edit files in services/payments/, but the indentation Claude uses is inconsistent.
question: What should the team do?

options.text: Nothing. A subdirectory CLAUDE.md fully replaces the root file for files in that folder.
Nothing. The root CLAUDE.md always takes priority, so 2 spaces will win in the end.
Scope the payments rule explicitly as an override for that directory.
Rename the payments file to CLAUDE.local.md so that Claude Code gives it a higher priority.

explanation.correct: CLAUDE.md files are concatenated, not overridden. The payments file loads once Claude works in that directory, so both rules sit in context and conflict. Making the payments rule explicit ("In services/payments/, indent with 4 spaces; this overrides the root rule") resolves the ambiguity.

distractors.A: Subdirectory files are added to context alongside the root file. They do not replace it.
distractors.B: There is no priority rule that makes the root file win. Both instructions are present and contradict each other.
distractors.D: CLAUDE.local.md is for personal, uncommitted notes. Renaming hides the rule from teammates and still leaves two conflicting instructions.

scenario: Four teams edit one 600-line project CLAUDE.md covering testing, API conventions, deployment, and security. Every section applies to all work in the repository, but the file causes constant merge conflicts and is hard to navigate.
question: How should the team reorganize it?

options.text: Keep one file, and add a table of contents at the top with links to each section.
Split it into topic files under .claude/rules/, such as testing.md and api.md.
Turn each section into a skill that Claude loads only when it judges one relevant.
Move each section into the CLAUDE.md files of the developers who maintain that area.

explanation.correct: .claude/rules/ holds topic-specific rule files. Rules without paths frontmatter load at launch, alongside the project CLAUDE.md, so behavior stays the same while each team owns a small file.

distractors.A: A table of contents helps navigation but leaves four teams editing one file, so the merge conflicts remain.
distractors.C: These rules apply to all work. Skills load on demand, so the rules would sometimes be missing.
distractors.D: Personal ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md files are not shared, so most of the team would lose the rules.

scenario: A team writes a /deploy-prod skill that runs their production release steps. They want it to run only when a developer types /deploy-prod, never because Claude decided on its own that it seemed relevant.
question: How should the skill be configured?

options.text: Write "never run this automatically" at the start of the skill's description.
Set user-invocable: false in the skill's frontmatter.
Set disable-model-invocation: true in the skill's frontmatter.
Move the release steps into the project CLAUDE.md file instead.

explanation.correct: disable-model-invocation: true stops Claude from loading the skill by itself. Developers can still run it with /deploy-prod. Its description is not even placed in context until the skill is invoked.

distractors.A: A note in the description is guidance Claude may or may not follow. The frontmatter flag is the documented control.
distractors.B: user-invocable: false does the opposite: it hides the skill from the / menu so only Claude can invoke it.
distractors.D: CLAUDE.md is always loaded, so the release steps would sit in context all the time and could be acted on unasked.

scenario: A /audit-deps skill scans every package manifest and prints hundreds of lines of findings into the main conversation. Developers run it in the middle of feature work and then find that Claude has lost track of earlier decisions.
question: What change helps most?

options.text: Add context: fork so the audit runs in a subagent; only its result returns.
Shorten the skill's instructions so that the skill itself takes up less context.
Tell developers to run /compact every time after they have used the skill.
Move the audit instructions into the project CLAUDE.md file instead.

explanation.correct: With context: fork, Claude Code runs the skill in a separate subagent context and returns its result, so the verbose output stays out of the main conversation.

distractors.B: The instructions are short. The bulk comes from the output the audit produces.
distractors.C: Compaction after the fact summarizes the noise along with the earlier decisions instead of keeping it out in the first place.
distractors.D: Moving the instructions to CLAUDE.md loads them in every session and still prints the output into the conversation.

scenario: A team adds context: fork to a /summarize-decisions skill that is meant to list the decisions made so far in the current conversation. Since the change, the skill returns generic advice that mentions none of the actual decisions.
question: What is the cause, and the fix?

options.text: The forked subagent runs on a smaller model, so set a stronger model in the agent field.
The skill needs an agent field naming a subagent type, so add one for the fork to use.
The instructions are too short for a subagent, so expand them with more detail on format.
A forked skill can't see the conversation, so remove context: fork from this skill.

explanation.correct: A forked skill runs as a subagent that receives the skill content as its prompt and does not see the conversation history. A skill whose job is to read the current conversation must run in the main context.

distractors.A: Model choice is not the problem. No model can summarize a conversation it was never given.
distractors.B: The agent field picks which subagent type runs the fork, but every forked subagent lacks the conversation history.
distractors.C: More instructions cannot replace the missing conversation, which is what the skill needs.

scenario: A team has two kinds of guidance: coding standards that apply to every change in the repository, and a 14-step release checklist that is used about once a week.
question: Where should each one live?

options.text: Both in the project CLAUDE.md, so that Claude always has all of the guidance in context.
Standards in the project CLAUDE.md, and the release checklist in a project skill.
Both as project skills, so Claude loads each one only when it seems relevant.
Standards in a project skill, and the release checklist in the project CLAUDE.md.

explanation.correct: CLAUDE.md is loaded in every session, which suits rules that apply to all work. A skill's body loads only when it is used, which suits an occasional multi-step procedure and keeps it from taking up context the rest of the week.

distractors.A: The checklist would cost context in every session for a task done weekly.
distractors.C: Standards that must always apply should not depend on Claude deciding they are relevant.
distractors.D: This swaps the two: always-needed rules would load on demand, and an occasional procedure would load all the time.

scenario: A team's /fix-issue skill needs an issue number to work. Developers often type /fix-issue without one, and Claude then spends a turn asking which issue they meant.
question: What frontmatter change helps developers supply the argument up front?

options.text: Rename the skill to /fix-issue-number so that the need is obvious.
Add a note about the required number to the project's CLAUDE.md.
Add argument-hint: [issue-number] to the frontmatter.
Have the skill tell Claude to pick the most recently opened issue.

explanation.correct: argument-hint shows the expected arguments in autocomplete as a developer types the command, so they see that an issue number is needed before sending.

distractors.A: A longer name hints at the need but is not a documented mechanism, and it makes the command harder to type.
distractors.B: CLAUDE.md is model context. It does not change what developers see while typing the command.
distractors.D: Guessing the issue risks working on the wrong one.

scenario: A team adds allowed-tools: Read Grep to the frontmatter of a /review skill, expecting this to stop Claude from running shell commands during reviews. During a review, Claude still asks to run a Bash command, and a developer approves it.
question: What explains this, and what would actually limit the tools?

options.text: It only pre-approves tools. Run the skill in a subagent limited to them.
allowed-tools is ignored in project skills and only takes effect in personal skills.
The field name is misspelled. Skills read allowedTools in camelCase, not allowed-tools.
allowed-tools applies only in non-interactive -p runs, never in interactive sessions.

explanation.correct: Per current docs, allowed-tools lists tools Claude can use without asking during the turn that invokes the skill. It grants permission and does not remove other tools. To limit tools, run the skill with context: fork using an agent whose tools list is restricted, or add permission deny rules.

distractors.B: Nothing in the docs limits allowed-tools to personal skills. It works the same way in project skills.
distractors.C: allowed-tools is the documented frontmatter field name for skills.
distractors.D: The field applies in interactive sessions too. It just means "don't ask", not "only these".

scenario: A developer created a personal ~/.claude/skills/deploy skill that differs from the team's project .claude/skills/deploy skill. When they type /deploy, their own version runs, and their deployments no longer match what teammates get.
question: What should the developer do?

options.text: Delete the team's project skill so that only one /deploy skill exists in total.
Rename the personal variant, so /deploy runs the team's version for everyone.
Move the personal variant into CLAUDE.local.md so that it stays out of git.
Add a priority: low field to the personal skill's frontmatter to rank it lower.

explanation.correct: When a personal skill and a project skill share a name, the personal one wins for that user. Giving the personal variant its own name, such as /deploy-sandbox, keeps it available without shadowing the team's /deploy.

distractors.A: Deleting the team's skill breaks /deploy for everyone else.
distractors.C: CLAUDE.local.md holds instructions, not invocable skills, so the variant would stop being a command.
distractors.D: There is no priority field for skills. Precedence is fixed by location.

scenario: Terraform conventions currently sit in the root CLAUDE.md and load in every session, even though most work never touches Terraform. The repository has Terraform files under infra/ and also in deploy/ folders inside many service directories.
question: What is the best way to load these conventions only when they are needed?

options.text: Keep them in the root CLAUDE.md, under a clearly marked Terraform heading.
Put a copy of the conventions in a CLAUDE.md in every folder with .tf files.
Add a .claude/rules/ file with paths: ["**/*.tf"] frontmatter.
Turn the conventions into a skill that developers run before editing Terraform.

explanation.correct: A rule with paths frontmatter loads only when Claude works with matching files, wherever they are. One glob covers .tf files in infra/ and in every service's deploy/ folder.

distractors.A: A heading does not change loading. The conventions still cost context in every session.
distractors.B: Copies in many folders drift apart, and new deploy folders need yet another copy.
distractors.D: A manually run skill depends on developers remembering it, while the rule applies automatically.

scenario: A rule in .claude/rules/migrations.md has paths: ["db/migrations/**/*.sql"]. A developer asks Claude a general question about the team's migration strategy, without referring to any migration file, and the answer ignores the rule.
question: What explains this?

options.text: Path-scoped rules load only once Claude works with a matching file.
Rules load only at session start, so the developer must restart Claude Code first.
Rules apply only after being imported into CLAUDE.md with an @ path reference.
Rule files in .claude/rules/ are only read while the session is in plan mode.

explanation.correct: A rule with paths is conditional: it loads when Claude works with files matching its patterns. A question that touches no migration file never triggers it. Referencing a migration file loads it, and if the rule should always apply, remove its paths field.

distractors.B: Unscoped rules load at launch, but path-scoped rules load on demand, so a restart would not help.
distractors.C: Rules in .claude/rules/ are discovered automatically and need no import.
distractors.D: Rules are not tied to plan mode.

scenario: A rule file starts with the frontmatter paths: [**/*.tsx], written without quotes. The team expected its React conventions to apply only to .tsx files, but the rule now appears in context in every session, even for backend-only work.
question: What is the most likely cause?

options.text: Claude Code ignores paths in project rules and only reads it in user-level rules.
Rule files must sit directly in .claude/rules/, not inside a subdirectory of it.
Rule files with frontmatter must use a .yaml extension instead of a .md one.
The YAML failed to parse, so the rule loaded unscoped. Quote the patterns.

explanation.correct: In YAML an unquoted * starts an alias, so this frontmatter does not parse. When frontmatter fails to parse, Claude Code ignores it and loads the rule as if it had no paths. Quoting the patterns (paths: ["**/*.tsx"]) fixes it, and claude --debug shows the parse error.

distractors.A: paths works in project rules. That is its main use.
distractors.B: Rule files are discovered recursively, so subdirectories such as frontend/ are fine.
distractors.C: Rules are Markdown files with YAML frontmatter. The .md extension is correct.

scenario: A developer has a failing test with a clear stack trace that points to a missing null check in one function of one file. The fix is obvious and touches about three lines.
question: How should they approach this with Claude Code?

options.text: Enter plan mode and have Claude produce a plan before it changes anything.
Have a subagent map the whole repository first to understand the context.
Use direct execution: ask Claude to add the null check and rerun the test.
Write a short design document first, then ask Claude to implement it.

explanation.correct: Direct execution suits small, well-understood changes with a clear scope. Here the cause is known and the change is local, so planning adds time without reducing risk.

distractors.A: Plan mode pays off for large or ambiguous changes. For a three-line fix with a clear stack trace it only adds a step.
distractors.B: Mapping the repository wastes time and context on a problem the stack trace already pinpoints.
distractors.D: A design document is far more process than a known three-line fix needs.

scenario: A team must replace a deprecated date library used in about 60 files. Some call sites could switch to native date APIs, others need a small adapter, and nobody knows yet how the usages split between the two.
question: How should they use Claude Code?

options.text: Plan mode to inventory usages and pick an approach, then execute the plan.
Ask Claude to convert all 60 files in one direct pass and fix failing tests afterwards.
Have four developers each convert 15 files in separate sessions, starting right away.
Convert only the files touched this sprint and leave the rest for some later sprint.

explanation.correct: This change spans many files and has more than one valid approach, so exploring first pays off. In plan mode Claude reads the code and proposes a plan without editing. Once the plan is approved, executing it directly is efficient.

distractors.B: Converting without knowing which approach fits each call site risks rework across 60 files.
distractors.C: Parallel sessions without a shared plan will choose different approaches for similar call sites.
distractors.D: Leaving the migration half done keeps both libraries in the codebase indefinitely.

scenario: During a multi-phase refactor, Claude's discovery phase (hundreds of search results and many file reads) fills most of the main conversation's context before any implementation begins.
question: What should the developer do in the next refactor?

options.text: Run /clear after discovery so that implementation starts with an empty context.
Switch to a model with a larger context window for the discovery phase.
Save the search results to a file and have Claude read that file back later.
Delegate discovery to a subagent that explores and returns only a summary.

explanation.correct: A subagent explores in its own context window and returns only its findings, so the main conversation keeps room for implementation. Claude Code's built-in Explore agent exists for this kind of read-only discovery.

distractors.A: Clearing discards the findings along with the noise, so implementation starts without what discovery learned.
distractors.B: A bigger window postpones the problem and still fills the main context with raw search output.
distractors.C: Reading the saved file back puts the same volume of output into the main context.

scenario: A team now runs every change through plan mode, including typo fixes and one-line config edits, and velocity has dropped. A senior engineer proposes dropping plan mode entirely and relying on code review instead.
question: Which policy fits best?

options.text: Keep plan mode for every change, since a plan never makes a change any less safe.
Plan for multi-file or multi-approach changes; go direct otherwise.
Drop plan mode entirely and rely on code review to catch the design problems instead.
Use plan mode only when a change will touch more than three files in the repository.

explanation.correct: Plan mode is for changes with architectural impact, several valid approaches, or many files. Small, clear changes are faster with direct execution. Deciding by those properties keeps the safety where it matters without slowing everything.

distractors.A: Planning trivial edits costs time with no benefit, which is the slowdown the team already has.
distractors.C: Code review catches problems after the work is done, when a wrong approach is expensive to undo.
distractors.D: File count is a crude proxy. A one-file change can need design work, and a mechanical change can touch many files.

scenario: An engineer wants Claude Code to analyze a repository of production configuration and propose changes. Nothing may be modified until a second engineer has reviewed the proposal.
question: What is the best way to run the session?

options.text: Use direct execution and put "do not edit any files" at the start of the prompt.
Use direct execution and rely on git to revert any edits Claude makes by mistake.
Use plan mode: Claude reads and proposes, but edits nothing until approved.
Make every file read-only on disk, then use direct execution as normal.

explanation.correct: In plan mode Claude reads files and proposes a plan but makes no edits until the plan is approved. You enter it with Shift+Tab or claude --permission-mode plan. That matches "analyze and propose, change nothing yet".

distractors.A: A prompt instruction is guidance, not a guarantee.
distractors.B: Reverting after the fact still allows unreviewed changes to land first.
distractors.D: Changing file permissions is a heavy workaround for what plan mode provides directly, and it is easy to forget to undo.

scenario: A developer describes in prose how legacy address strings should be normalized. Each time Claude implements it, the result differs in small ways, such as abbreviations and the order of the parts.
question: What is the most effective next step?

options.text: Rewrite the prose description so that it is longer and much more detailed.
Give two or three concrete input and expected-output examples.
Ask Claude to take extra care and to double-check its work every time.
Switch to a different model that may read the prose more consistently.

explanation.correct: When prose is read inconsistently, a few concrete input/output pairs remove the ambiguity. They show exactly how to handle abbreviations and ordering.

distractors.A: More prose usually adds more ways to interpret it.
distractors.C: "Take care" adds no information about what the right output is.
distractors.D: The ambiguity lives in the specification, not the model.

scenario: A team needs a rate limiter with tricky edge cases: bursts at window boundaries, clock skew, and a requirement to handle 10,000 checks per second. Earlier attempts looked right in review but failed in production.
question: Which workflow fits best?

options.text: Have Claude write the limiter, then ask Claude whether it handles all the edge cases.
Describe the edge cases in prose, then review the code Claude writes line by line.
Have Claude write the limiter and its tests together, and trust that the tests pass.
Write tests for behavior, edge cases, and throughput first; iterate on failures.

explanation.correct: Tests written first define the behavior, edge cases, and performance requirement objectively. Claude then iterates against real failures, which you share back each round, instead of against a reading of prose.

distractors.A: Asking whether the code is right gets an opinion, not evidence.
distractors.B: Line-by-line review is how the earlier attempts slipped through.
distractors.C: Tests written alongside the code tend to share its blind spots.

scenario: A developer has to add a caching layer to a pricing service but has never designed caches before. They worry about missing something important, such as how prices are invalidated, or what happens when the cache is down.
question: How should they start the session with Claude?

options.text: Ask Claude to interview them about requirements before coding.
Ask Claude to implement a cache right away, then fix the problems as they show up.
Paste in a generic caching tutorial and ask Claude to follow it step by step.
Tell Claude to be thorough and to think of everything while it implements.

explanation.correct: Having Claude ask questions first (the interview pattern) surfaces considerations the developer did not know to mention, such as invalidation rules, staleness limits, and failure modes, before any code exists.

distractors.B: In an unfamiliar domain, fixing problems as they appear means discovering design flaws late.
distractors.C: A generic tutorial cannot cover this service's pricing and invalidation needs.
distractors.D: "Think of everything" does not reveal what the developer actually needs.

scenario: Reviewing a data-migration script, a developer finds three problems. Null dates crash the parser. The date-format fix changes which rows reach the null-handling path. And there is an unrelated typo in a log message.
question: How should they give Claude the feedback?

options.text: Send one issue per message, in the order they were found, whatever the dependency.
Collect every comment on the whole repository and send all of them in one message.
Send the two linked problems together; send the typo separately.
Fix the two linked problems by hand and ask Claude only to correct the log typo.

explanation.correct: Issues that interact should be described together, so Claude can design one consistent fix. Independent issues can be handled separately. The null and date problems interact; the typo does not.

distractors.A: Fixing the date format alone changes the null path. One at a time invites back-and-forth and rework.
distractors.B: Unrelated comments from across the repository dilute the message and blur which problems interact.
distractors.D: Doing the hard part by hand gives up Claude's help where it is most useful.

scenario: A CI job runs Claude Code on each pull request and posts findings as inline comments. The script currently asks Claude to "respond in JSON" and parses the text, which breaks whenever Claude adds a sentence before the JSON.
question: What is the most reliable fix?

options.text: Add "respond with only JSON and nothing else" to the prompt in capital letters.
Use --output-format stream-json and extract the JSON with a regular expression.
Run the job with --verbose so the output contains complete debugging details.
Use --output-format json with --json-schema; read structured_output.

explanation.correct: With --output-format json and --json-schema, the response carries schema-conforming data in structured_output, separate from any prose. The script should check the field exists, because a run that ends without valid output leaves it out.

distractors.A: Stronger wording makes clean JSON more likely, but parsing still breaks on the occasional extra sentence.
distractors.B: stream-json gives event lines, not schema-validated findings, so the regular expression stays fragile.
distractors.C: --verbose adds detail to the output. It does not structure the findings.

scenario: A CI review job runs again on every new commit to a pull request. Each run reposts comments the previous run already made about issues the author has not fixed yet, so pull requests fill up with duplicate comments.
question: What change addresses this best?

options.text: Pass the previous findings; ask for only new or still-open issues.
Delete all earlier review comments before every run and repost them from scratch.
Run the review only on the first commit of each pull request and never again.
Drop new comments whose text exactly matches a comment that was posted before.

explanation.correct: Giving Claude the prior findings lets it report only new issues and ones that remain open, which keeps the thread readable and still catches regressions.

distractors.B: Deleting and reposting erases the discussion history on each comment.
distractors.C: Reviewing only the first commit misses problems introduced later.
distractors.D: Claude rarely words a finding the same way twice, so exact-text matching misses most duplicates.

scenario: A team has Claude Code generate a feature and then, in the same session, asks it to review its own changes. The reviews rarely find problems, yet human reviewers keep catching subtle bugs afterwards.
question: What change would most improve the reviews?

options.text: Ask the same session to review its code a second time, much more carefully.
Turn on more reasoning effort for the review step within the same session.
Review in a separate, fresh Claude instance that didn't write the code.
Ask the session to list any doubts it had while it was writing the code.

explanation.correct: A session that wrote the code carries its own reasoning and assumptions, which makes it less likely to question them. An independent instance without that context reviews the change as written.

distractors.A: A second pass in the same session repeats the same blind spots.
distractors.B: More effort within the same context still reasons from the same assumptions.
distractors.D: Self-reported doubts show what the session noticed, not what it missed.

scenario: Following the docs' advice for CI, a team runs claude --bare -p for automated test generation. The generated tests ignore the fixture and naming conventions written in the project's CLAUDE.md, although the same prompt follows them in interactive sessions.
question: What explains this, and what is the fix?

options.text: CLAUDE.md never loads in -p mode, so the team must stop running Claude Code in CI.
--bare skips CLAUDE.md, so pass the conventions with --append-system-prompt-file.
CI runners cannot read dotfiles, so the CLAUDE.md file must be renamed for CI.
Test generation ignores project context, so add the conventions to every test prompt.

explanation.correct: Bare mode skips auto-discovery of hooks, skills, MCP servers, auto memory, and CLAUDE.md, so CI runs are reproducible across machines. Context has to be passed explicitly, for example with --append-system-prompt-file pointing at the conventions. Without --bare, -p loads CLAUDE.md as usual.

distractors.A: -p loads CLAUDE.md normally. It is --bare that skips it.
distractors.C: CLAUDE.md is not a dotfile, and the runner can read it. Bare mode chooses not to.
distractors.D: Pasting the conventions into every prompt works but duplicates them. The documented route is a system prompt file.

scenario: A nightly job runs claude -p "Run the test suite and fix any failures". Logs show Claude tried to run npm test several times, but each call was denied, and the job ended without running a single test.
question: What should the team change?

options.text: Pre-approve the test command with --allowedTools "Bash(npm test *)".
Add a line to CLAUDE.md saying Claude may run the test suite in CI.
Run the job interactively so someone can approve each command it needs.
Use --permission-mode bypassPermissions so that nothing ever asks.

explanation.correct: In a -p run, calls that need approval are denied unless something approves them. --allowedTools with permission rule syntax pre-approves exactly the commands the job needs, here npm test with any arguments.

distractors.B: CLAUDE.md is instructions, not permissions, so the calls would still be denied.
distractors.C: A nightly job has nobody to approve commands.
distractors.D: Bypassing every permission is far broader than the job needs, and the docs reserve it for isolated environments.

scenario: A nightly CI job asks Claude Code to add tests for recently changed modules. Developers find that many generated tests duplicate scenarios the existing suite already covers, and others ignore the team's shared fixtures.
question: What change most improves the generated tests?

options.text: Ask Claude to generate twice as many tests so that more of them end up being new.
Delete generated tests whose names match existing ones after every nightly run.
Switch the job to a different model for test generation only, keeping the prompt.
Give it the existing tests; document fixtures and standards in CLAUDE.md.

explanation.correct: Claude can only avoid duplicates it can see, so the existing tests for each module belong in context. Documenting the testing standards and available fixtures in CLAUDE.md (or passing them explicitly when running with --bare) steers new tests toward real gaps and the team's conventions.

distractors.A: More tests produce more duplicates, and more noise for reviewers.
distractors.B: Matching names misses duplicates with different names, and does nothing about the ignored fixtures.
distractors.C: The problem is missing context, not the model.
